records.title: Volatile and Non‐Volatile Ferroelectric HZO for Low‐Power Reservoir Computing
records.abstract: ABSTRACT We present a capacitive reservoir computing system based on hafnium‐zirconium oxide (HZO) capacitors that integrates intrinsically volatile and non‐volatile functionalities within a single material platform. Through compositional control, fabricated Hf 0 . 8 Zr 0 . 2 O 2 provides stable ferroelectric (FE) behavior for non‐volatile weight storage, whereas Hf 0 . 2 Zr 0 . 8 O 2 exhibits volatile antiferroelectric‐like (VFE) dynamics characterized by fading memory and nonlinear responses. Using polarization‐voltage, capacitance‐voltage, and dynamic transient measurements from these devices, we formulate and calibrate a modified Landau‐Khalatnikov compact model that accurately reproduces both FE and VFE switching behaviors. Implemented and validated in Cadence Spectre, the model enables realistic large‐scale circuit simulations. Leveraging this framework, a hybrid reservoir network combining an FE HZO capacitor array with transistor‐coupled VFE HZO nodes was developed. Co‐simulation between Python‐based system evaluation and Cadence circuit modeling achieves 93.5% accuracy on the Voice‐MNIST classification task with ultralow energy consumption (∼184 fJ per cell and ∼1.07 pJ per node per inference). These results establish a unified HZO‐based device‐circuit‐system framework for scalable, CMOS‐compatible, and energy‐efficient temporal neuromorphic computing.
records.authors: Yichun Xu; Davide Rossetti; Shiva Asapu; Taehwan Moon; Jian Zhao; Ruoyu Zhao; Seung Ju Kim; Tong Wang; Michele Bonnin; Alon Ascoli; Andreu Glasmann; Sina Najmaei; Fernando Corinto; R. Stanley Williams; J. Joshua Yang

records.title: Multimodal Reservoir Computing Enabled by a Single Ferroelectric Heterojunction With Bio‐Inspired Visual–Olfactory Fusion
records.abstract: ABSTRACT Brain‐inspired computing based on emerging devices offers a route to bypass the von Neumann bottleneck and enables efficient parallel data processing. Bismuth‐based perovskite oxides, which combine ferroelectric, optoelectronic, and semiconducting properties, represent compelling candidates for information‐processing substrates, yet their multifunctional synergies remain underexplored. Here, we demonstrate a dual‐terminal multifunctional sensory synapse based on a single all‐Aurivillius‐phase Bi 2 WO 6 /SrBi 2 Ta 2 O 9 ferroelectric heterojunction that exhibits tunable spatiotemporal dynamics under optical and gaseous stimuli. The interplay among ferroelectric polarization, oxygen‐vacancy migration, and charge trapping/detrapping enables heterosynaptic plasticity with relaxation times scalable via stimulus intensity. We further emulate bio‐inspired visual–olfactory fusion perception and leverage these dynamics to construct a multimodal reservoir computing framework. The system achieves efficient, high‐accuracy image recognition through in‐sensor volatile‐to‐non‐volatile transformation and programmable cross‐modal integration, maintaining robust performance under stochastic noise (up to 50%). This work presents a co‐designed framework that fuses multimodal perceptual intelligence with brain‐inspired computing, offering a scalable pathway toward future adaptive human–machine interaction.
records.authors: Liping Tan; X.-R. Hu; Mudan Feng; Ming Zhou; Along Li; Zi Wang; Shuang Zhao; Xiaoliang Wang; Peipei Li; Weiwei Qin; Yali Bi; Wei Zhang

records.title: Embodied Hydrodynamic Reservoir Computing for Underwater Obstacle Localization
records.abstract: In underwater environments, fluid–structure interactions can provide detailed information about the surroundings. However, exploiting these hydrodynamic responses as a contactless sensing mechanism for obstacle localization remains challenging. Existing approaches often require complicated sensors or data processing methods to operate reliably in underwater environments. This study presents the design and performance evaluation of three embodied soft panels, inspired by the physiology and sensory setup of a fish's body. We demonstrate that embodied intelligence can be achieved by using a framework called physical reservoir computing (PRC), which utilizes the physical body dynamics as a computational resource. Herein, the 3D-printed panels with embedded sensing networks were designed for the pur pose of extracting their body-state information for embodied computation. The nonlinear autoregressive moving average (NARMA) task was used to evaluate their computational per formance. We show that under appropriate physical reservoir dynamics, the panels exhibited greater capability to emulate nonlinear dynamical systems and function as physical reservoir computers. Furthermore, we also show that the panels had enough computational power to estimate the position of a nearby obstacle based on variations in their body dynamics. Our results suggest that the panels can serve as potential frameworks for intelligent swimmers capable of perceiving their environments through the self-sensing mechanism and estimating relevant information.
records.authors: Ken Kanate Wichiramala

records.title: Interfacial and Bulk Switching MoS 2 Memristors for an All-2D Reservoir Computing Framework
records.abstract: In this study, we report non-filamentary resistance switching with short- and long-term memory dynamics in Au/Ti/MoS 2 /Au memristive devices. The temporal dynamics is engineered by controlling the thickness of the chemical-vapor-deposited (CVD) MoS 2 films. Monolayer (1L)-MoS 2 devices exhibit forming-free and unipolar resistance switching with short-term memory (STM). Bipolar and non-volatile resistance switching with outstanding cycle-to-cycle uniformity is observed for the multilayer (ML) MoS 2 memristive devices. Detailed transport analysis and high-resolution scanning tunneling electron microscopy (HRSTEM) studies correlate the non-volatile switching in ML-MoS 2 with a trap-assisted space charge limited conduction (SCLC) mechanism, leading to a bulk-limited resistance switching behavior. We fabricate a 16 × 16 array of ML-MoS 2 memristors and demonstrate long-term potentiation/depression behavior. The 1L-MoS 2 memristive devices with STM are used to generate four-bit reservoir states. Finally, we simulate a small reservoir computing (RC) framework by using experimental data from 5 reservoir neurons and the 16 × 16 synaptic array. This small RC network achieves 89.56% accuracy in a spoken-digit recognition task, owing to the excellent cycle-to-cycle uniformity in both the reservoir neurons and the synaptic array. Our work demonstrates the possibility of creating neural networks with reliable performance using non-filamentary memristive devices on a single 2D-material platform.
records.authors: Asmita S. Thool; Sourodeep Roy; Prahalad Kanti Barman; Kartick Biswas; Pavan Nukala; Abhishek Misra; Saptarshi Das; Bhaswar Chakrabarti

records.title: Minimizing Stochastic Complexity with Ridge Regression
records.abstract: We derive a penalty strength criterion for ridge regression using stochastic complexity, which is a refined variant of the minimum description length principle. Since stochastic complexity does not typically account for the effect of regularization on complexity, despite its ability to simplify models, we are required to make a slight modification to the underlying coding scheme. Our scheme makes use of a weighted ensemble of regularized model fits rather than a mixture of maximum likelihood estimates. Under this modification, regularization is interpreted as reducing model complexity by constraining flexibility. In the case of ridge regression, the complexity penalty term that we derive can be expressed analytically as the log determinant of the residual operator. We demonstrate the effect of this complexity penalty by fitting a linear readout to a reservoir computer, and by performing benchmark testing on publicly available datasets.
records.authors: Antony Mizzi; David M. Walker; MICHAEL P. SMALL

records.title: Are language models models?
records.abstract: Futrell and Mahowald claim language models (LMs) "serve as model systems," but an assessment at each of Marr's three levels suggests the claim is clearly not true at the implementation level, poorly motivated at the algorithmic-representational level, and problematic at the computational theory level. LMs are good candidates as tools; calling them cognitive models overstates the case and unnecessarily feeds large language model hype.
records.authors: Philip Resnik

records.title: Performance of Chaotic Time Series Prediction Using a Spiking Reservoir with an Excitation Layer and an Inhibition Layer
records.abstract: In this study, a structural design is investigated to improve the stability of the autonomous prediction of chaotic time series using a spiking neural network (SNN) as a reservoir. A two-layer SNN reservoir composed of excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) neurons is constructed, and the prediction output is learned by updating only the readout weights online using FORCE. Using the Lorenz system as a benchmark, normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) is evaluated by separating the training (teacher-forcing) and closed-loop autonomous segments; the results indicate that the two-layer architecture reproduces key waveform features and that the autonomous-segment prediction accuracy varies with the E/I ratio.
records.authors: Tomoki Goto; Yoko Uwate; Yoshifumi Nishio

records.title: Softening-hardening transition in landslide slip zones under cyclic reservoir fluctuations: Insights into the deformation evolution process
records.abstract: Reservoir landslides exhibit pronounced sensitivity to cyclic water-level fluctuations, yet current models often fail to capture the effect of cyclic loading induced by long-term reservoir water fluctuations, remaining constrained by static assumptions. This study bridges the knowledge gap by conducting triaxial tests that simulate reservoir-induced cyclic loading. By comparing the strain difference between the slip zone soil under cyclic and static loading methods, the deformation characteristics of slip zone soil under different stress levels ( SL ), over-consolidation ratios ( OCR ), and loading frequencies ( f ) were analyzed, and the deformation behaviors of the specimens were classified according to the cyclic softening/hardening coefficient index. The results indicate that the strain evolution mechanism under cyclic loading is fundamentally different from that under static creep. Unlike the cyclic loading associated with traffic and earthquake, the soil strain under reservoir cyclic loading exhibits a softening-hardening transition mechanism with clear stress dependence. An integrated SL , OCR , and f model, along with a cumulative plastic strain model, was developed and validated with experimental data and actual reservoir monitoring data, respectively. These findings provide pioneer systematic investigation into the cyclic loading effects of landslides in reservoir areas and offer a paradigm shift in reservoir landslide risk assessment, enabling dynamic stability evaluations aligned with operational water-level fluctuations.
records.authors: Xiaoxi Wang; Xicheng Zhang; Huiming Tang; Qiong Wu; Li Jiang
records.venue: Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering

records.title: Volatile Memristor-Based Artificial Spiking Neurons for Bioinspired Computing
records.abstract: The report reviews recent research efforts in demonstrating a computing system whose operation principle mimics the dynamics of biological neurons. The temporal variation of the membrane potential of neurons is one of the key features that contribute to the information processing in the brain. We first summarize the neuron models that explain the experimentally observed change in the membrane potential. The function of ion channels is briefly introduced to understand such change from the molecular viewpoint. Dedicated circuits that can simulate the neuronal dynamics have been developed to reproduce the charging and discharging dynamics of neurons depending on the input ionic current from presynaptic neurons. Key elements include volatile memristors that can undergo volatile resistance switching depending on the voltage bias. This behavior called the threshold switching has been utilized to reproduce the spikes observed in the biological neurons. Various types of threshold switch have been applied in a different configuration in the hardware demonstration of neurons. Recent studies revealed that the memristor-based circuits could provide energy and space efficient options for the demonstration of neurons using the innate physical properties of materials compared to the options demonstrated with the conventional complementary metal-oxidesemiconductors (CMOS).

records.title: Enhancing nonlinear computational capacity in simple cycle reservoir with time-varying connectivity
records.abstract: Reservoir computing (RC) is an efficient framework for temporal signal processing in which only the readout layer is trained. Recently, physical implementations of RC have attracted increasing attention for energy-efficient and high-speed computation. In such physical systems, complex network structures are difficult to implement due to hardware constraints, even though the network topology plays a critical role in determining computational performance. Among various reservoir architectures, simple cycle reservoir (SCR) is well suited for hardware implementation due to its minimal connectivity and strong memory capability. However, its unidirectional ring structure inherently limits long-range information propagation, thereby reducing its ability to capture complex temporal dependencies. To overcome this structural limitation, we propose a reconfigurable SCR framework with a time-varying connectivity design. Selective rewiring enhances information propagation, while temporal switching among topologies increases dynamical diversity. Experimental results show that increasing the number of shortcut connections enhances second-order information processing capacity. Temporal topology switching further reduces prediction error in the NARMA10 benchmark task. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves computational capability while preserving hardware efficiency.
records.authors: Shimon Matsuno; Kota Ando; Tetsuya Asai
records.venue: Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications IEICE

records.title: Device Variability and Uncertainty Propagation in Memristive Reservoir Computing
records.abstract: Memristive crossbar arrays provide an efficient hardware substrate for in-memory and neuromorphic computing architectures. Reservoir Computing (RC) is particularly well suited for such systems because only the output layer requires training, making it attractive for hardware implementations. However, memristive devices exhibit intrinsic variability due to fabrication mismatch, cycle-to-cycle fluctuations, and conductance drift, which introduce stochasticity in the reservoir dynamics. In this work we develop a probabilistic formulation of memristive reservoir computing that explicitly models conductance variability in the crossbar array. Analytical expressions are derived to describe how device uncertainty propagates through the reservoir states and determines the predictive distribution at the readout layer. This framework enables the analysis of dynamical regimes in which hardware variability either degrades performance or can instead enhance the diversity of the reservoir dynamics. The theoretical results are validated through numerical experiments on chaotic time-series prediction tasks, including the Mackey–Glass benchmark, showing how device variability affects both prediction accuracy and predictive uncertainty. These results provide theoretical insight into uncertainty propagation in memristive reservoirs and establish connections between variability-aware reservoir computing and stochastic random feature methods.
records.authors: Davide Rossetti; Fernando Corinto
records.venue: International Conference on Modern Circuits and Systems Technologies

records.title: Halide perovskite devices for unconventional computing
records.abstract: In the present data-centric age, ubiquitous intelligent electronics have seen a meteoric proliferation. These electronics are equipped with arrays of multimodal sensors that enable them to perceive and interact with the physical world. However, the present computing framework has been unable to manage the exponentially increasing amount of data being produced by these sensors. This is known as the data deluge problem, which has prompted researchers to rethink how data from sensors is processed. Sensors are typically deployed in areas with minimal computational capacity (known as the edge). Hence, the conventional computing paradigm has adopted a centralized framework. Here, the data generated from the sensors is communicated to a data centre (or cloud) where the data is stored and processed to make a consolidated decision. However, in this framework, data communication consumes several orders of magnitude more energy than the computation step. Moreover, communicating such vast quantities of data also increases decision-making latency. To address this bottleneck, inspiration can be drawn from the biological information processing paradigm, which relies on a hierarchical computing framework. Here, computation is distributed rather than centralized, with low-level computations performed near the sensory receptors to extract meaningful data from the raw stimulus. This reduces the amount of data that must be communicated to the brain for consolidated decision-making. To implement unconventional computing in electronics, innovation is required in novel device physics and architectures, as well as in materials that enable them. This establishes the dissertation's key challenge. Halide perovskites are a class of semiconductors renowned for their remarkable optoelectronic properties, including a high absorption coefficient in the visible-to-near-infrared region, high ambipolar carrier diffusion lengths and mobilities, and defect tolerance. Consequently, they have taken the center stage in thin-film photovoltaics. Moreover, due to their low formation energy, highly crystalline films can be solution-processed at low temperatures. Interestingly, this leads to the formation of weak bonds and soft lattices, which unveil a unique phenomenon. The soft lattice enables ions and charged vacancies within the crystal to migrate in response to electrical, optical, or thermal stimuli without disrupting the crystal lattice. This property is detrimental to photovoltaic applications as it results in anomalous phenomena such as current-voltage hysteresis due to the complex interplay between ionic and electronic carriers. However, this anomaly has recently received attention from the neuromorphic community, as these complex carrier dynamics can be leveraged to mimic artificial synapses and neurons. This thesis aims to synergize the optoelectronic properties and complex ionic-electronic dynamics of halide perovskites for devices for in-sensor and near-sensor computing systems. First, a halide perovskite solar cell has been used as a self-powered short-term optically stimulated memory. Using the non-linear dynamics of the transient open-circuit voltage, in-sensor reservoir computing has been proposed for pre-processing optical time-series. A potential use case of cardiac health monitoring and anomaly detection was proposed. Then, a halide perovskite solar cell-like device has been used as an analog, filament-free non-volatile memristor for near-sensor computing. A preconditioning step for the memristor, known as electrochemical doping, has been proposed. The preconditioning step enhanced the ohmic window of the memristor and reduced the capacitive transient effects. 5 bits of multistate retention, stable for >1000 seconds, was achieved using this approach. By using these memristors in a crossbar array configuration for vector matrix multiplication, the near-sensor task of principal component analysis could be performed. Finally, one of the key limitations of halide perovskites, ambient degradation, was addressed in a filamentary non-volatile memristor. A novel approach to encapsulating halide perovskites while preserving device operation was introduced by using the self-assembled nanostructures of a block copolymer as a crystallization template. Devices able to withstand ambient conditions (25 °C, 85% RH) for over 60 days were obtained. Moreover, the devices could retain the conductance states for over 10,000 seconds at 85 °C.
records.authors: Divyam Sharma

records.title: DESIGN OF CMOS-MEMRISTOR CIRCUIT OF LSTM ARCHITECTUR
records.abstract: The growing amount of data, the dawn of Moore's law, and the need for machines with human intelligence dictated several new concepts in computing and chip design. Existing physical limitations of Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) transistors and von-Neumann bottleneck problems showed that there is a need for the development of in-memory computing devices using technologies beyond-CMOS. The architecture of the long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network makes it an ideal candidate for modern computing systems. Recurrent connections and built-in memory of the LSTM network also allow us to process different types of data, including ones with temporal features and dependency. The realization of LSTM, and other artificial neural networks (ANNs), implies a large amount of parallel computations. Therefore, in most cases, their training and inferencing are implemented on modern computing systems with the help of a graphical processing unit (GPU). In addition, there are several available solutions for energy and area efficient inference of neural networks based on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA) and application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) platforms in both digital and analog domains. In 2008, the discovery of a new device called 'memristor’, which acts as an artificial synapse, brought attention to developments of memristive artificial neural networks ANNs. Due to their nanoscale size and non-volatile nature, memristor crossbar arrays (MCA) allow several orders of magnitude faster dot-product multiplication and require a smaller area and lower energy consumption. The recent successful works where memristors were used as a dot-product engine include “A convolutional neural network accelerator with in-situ analog arithmetic in crossbars” (ISAAC) and “A programmable ultra-efficient memristor-based accelerator for machine learning inference” (PUMA). Nevertheless, training of ANN on FPGA and ASIC remains a challenging problem. Therefore, the majority of memristive platforms are proposed only for the acceleration of neural networks with pre-trained parameters. In this thesis work, the design of an analog CMOS-memristor accelerator implementing long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network at the edge is proposed. The circuit design of a single LSTM unit consists of two main parts: 1) a dot-product engine based on memristor crossbar array using “one weight -two memristors” scheme; and 2) CMOS circuit blocks used to realize arithmetic and non-linear functions within LSTM unit. The proposed design was validated on machine learning problems such as prediction and classification. The performance of the analog LSTM circuit design was compared with other types of neural networks and neuromorphic systems, including a single perceptron, FNN, DNN, and modified HTM. Besides, analyses of memristor state variability in hybrid CNN-LSTM and CNN implementation for image classification have been performed successfully.

records.title: Evolutionary Echo State Network Architecture Search for Time-Series Prediction
records.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs) are efficient recurrent models for temporal dynamics, but their performance depends strongly on component choice, architecture, and hyperparameters, which are often selected manually or optimized separately. We propose Evolutionary ESN Architecture Search (EESNAS), a hybrid framework that uses a genetic algorithm for structural exploration and Bayesian optimization for local hyperparameter refinement. EESNAS is evaluated on six benchmark time-series tasks under one-step and autoregressive protocols against reservoir-computing, recurrent-network, and ablation baselines. It improves predictive accuracy and run-to-run stability on most datasets while remaining practical relative to exhaustive hyperparameter search. Statistical comparisons and ablations show that structural search and hyperparameter tuning provide complementary, dataset-dependent gains, supporting coordinated empirical adaptation of ESN topology, component choice, and local hyperparameters.

records.title: From population to coherence: modeling, optimization, and application of atomic vapor for information storage
records.abstract: Multimode optical memories are a fundamental requirement for several emerging technologies. In optical neural networks, classical optical memories provide low-latency data input and buffer optical information awaiting processing. In quantum information processing, memories are key for storing and synchronizing quantum states to enable high-fidelity, secure communication and authentication protocols. This thesis investigates the use of an Optically writable Random Access Memory (ORAM) based on warm cesium (Cs) vapor across both classical and quantum applications. A Cs vapor presents an ideal candidate for both classical and quantum memory due to its potential for long-lived ground-state storage, readily accessible multimode capacity, and reduced technical overhead. Our investigation begins in the classical regime, exploring the operation of an incoherent ORAM based on atomic population pumping. We experimentally implement this memory and integrate it into a machine learning architecture as a novel optical reservoir computer. By evaluating the memory against standard benchmarking tasks, we identify the physical constraints responsible for its limited memory capacity and critically assess its practical viability for reservoir computing. Following this classical demonstration, the focus shifts to the coherent storage of quantum information. We introduce a quantum channel formalism to model warm vapor quantum memories, and use it to evaluate the critical figures of merit necessary for secure applications such as quantum tokens. To address the performance requirements set by different quantum information processing applications, we present a series of experiments optimizing memory efficiency, noise, and multimode capacity. This includes deploying an in-situ machine learning algorithm to optimize temporal control pulses, experimentally confirming theoretical models of pulse shaping. By contrasting both the incoherent and coherent platforms, we outline the specific experimental advancements required to reach application-ready optical memories in a warm Cs vapor. The contributions presented in this thesis can be summarized as follows: - The formulation and investigation of incoherent atomic pumping as a means of classical optical storage. - The first use of a warm Cs vapor as a randomly addressable classical memory in a reservoir computing system. - A channel formalism implementation of atomic ensemble quantum memories, with performance analyses comparing the behavior of different state-of-the-art memory experiments. - The simultaneous optimization of several experimental quantum memory parameters, including the demonstration of a random-access spatially multiplexed coherent memory in a warm Cs vapor. - The first demonstration of an in-experiment machine learning algorithm simultaneously optimizing the efficiency and pulse energy in a warm atomic vapor. This thesis provides new insights into the practical capabilities of multimode warm vapor memories, establishing a foundation for their continued development across both classical and quantum information processing regimes.

records.title: Advancing Halide Perovskite RRAMs: From Enhanced Stability to Multifunctional Applications
records.abstract: The application of halide perovskites (HPs) in resistive random access memories (RRAMs) has historically been constrained by material and electrical instability in HP thin-film devices, leading to suboptimal figures-of-merit (FOMs) such as retention, endurance, and switching speed. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an innovative switching matrix that replaces the traditional thin-film architecture with vertically aligned, three-dimensional, high-density monocrystalline HP nanowires and quantum wires embedded in a porous alumina membrane (PAM), positioned between metal contacts. This PAM offers exceptional passivation, significantly enhancing the electrical and material stability of the environmentally sensitive HPs by minimizing surface diffusion pathways and preventing moisture-induced degradation. Our approach achieved unprecedented retention times of up to 28.3 years, device endurance of 5 million cycles, and switching speeds as rapid as 100 picoseconds, marking the best FOMs reported for HP RRAMs. In stark contrast, HP thin-film devices for data storage applications have shown a maximum endurance of 10,000 cycles, retention of 105 seconds, and switching speeds of 10 nanoseconds. Furthermore, we fabricated a 14 nm lateral size HP quantum wire RRAM cell and developed a cross-bar device architecture with a novel metal-semiconductor-insulator-metal (MSIM) based sneaky path mitigation scheme, demonstrating the scalability potential of our devices. Beyond data storage, we pioneered HP-based physical neural networks using nanowires and quantum wires in PAM, achieving low power and high precision computing capabilities. Devices were operated in two modes: electro-chemical metallization (ECM) with a silver top electrode and non-electro-chemical metallization (non-ECM) with an indium tin oxide top electrode. These multi-level states were used to adjust weights or conductance values in artificial neural networks for various image processing tasks, including outlining, sharpening, and embossing in ECM mode. In non-ECM mode, we emulated the cognitive learning model of the Gestalt Closure Principle. Additionally, we extended our approach to a perovskite-based artificial vision system that integrates a physical pre-processor with a physical processor, demonstrating reliable photo-synaptic behavior and stable, temporally robust conduction states. The devices exhibit retention greater than 105 seconds and temporal jitter below 10%, while also responding to changes in light intensity, duration, and frequency, enabling contrast enhancement. Finally, we successfully recognized four distinct geometric shapes using a 6×6 array of nanowire devices. In summary, these groundbreaking findings elevate HP RRAMs to a state-of-the-art standard and highlight the potential of perovskite nanowire and quantum wire devices as a promising alternative technology for future storage and computing modules.

records.title: Improving Deep Learning Efficiency Using Reservoir Computing Inspiration
records.abstract: Forefront deep learning (DL) models involve massive computation and energy costs due to their vast number of parameters and intensive use of power-hungry arithmetic operations.Recently, AI commercial applications have experienced rapid growth in adoption, elevating this problem to a source of environmental concern.Although there have been multiple efforts to optimize DL at both the algorithmic and hardware fronts, there is an ongoing trend for exponentially larger models.Alternatively, research in various emerging technologies has explored solutions in different machine learning schemes and novel computation substrates.Among them, reservoir computing (RC) has emerged as a promising alternative by proving its high efficiency in early experiments.This records.title: Photonic Reservior Computing or Real-Time Malware Detection in Encrypted Network Traffic
records.abstract: The development of encrypted network traffic has brought huge improvements to user privacy but has paradoxically introduced huge difficulties in the detection of real time malware attack traffic, since the traditional methods used to inspect payloads are rendered useless. Existing machine learning and deep learning models in the field of encrypted traffic analysis are, in particular, plagued by high computation costs, latency problems and poor scalability when deployed to high throughput networks. Photonic Reservoir Computing (PRC) is a new paradigm based on exploiting the nonlinear dynamics of optical systems that could represent an interesting alternative to the current paradigm, enabling ultra-fast, low-latency and energy-efficient data processing. This study investigates the use of PRC in identifying malware in the encrypted traffic by encoding flow-level statistical features into the photonic reservoirs for classification. The results show that PRC not only offers competitive detection accuracy in comparison to standard deep learning techniques but also shows better real-time performance and energy efficiency characteristics, and is suitable for deployment in large scale in Internet Service Providers (ISPs), critical infrastructures and IoT ecosystems. The results of this research make PRC a promising transformative strategy for next-generation intrusion detection systems to meet the dual challenges of privacy and security.

records.title: Reconfigurable Phononic Metastructures for Physical Computing and Mechano-Intelligence
records.abstract: Recent advances in autonomous engineering systems are creating growing demands for next-generation intelligent material and structural systems that can perceive their surroundings, store and process information, make decisions, and adapt to changing conditions. Conventionally, these capabilities are realized by integrating external electronics and digital platforms. Although powerful, it separates intelligence from the physical body that interacts with the environment and can introduce complexity, energy overhead, latency, and vulnerability under harsh or resource-limited environments. This motivates the emerging concepts of mechano-intelligence, where intelligent functions are embodied directly within the mechanics of architected structures. However, existing efforts have largely focused on isolated and narrowly defined functions, and a systematic framework for integrating different aspects of mechano-intelligence remains lacking. This dissertation addresses this challenge by establishing physical computing as a foundational framework for advancing mechano-intelligence in and through reconfigurable phononic metastructures. The central objective is to harness the unique mechanical and wave characteristics of these systems to pursue physical reservoir computing and wave-based computing, so as to create and integrate key elements of intelligence—perception, memory, learning, decision-making, and adaptation—within the mechanical domain. Specifically, the dissertation first develops a new physical reservoir computing framework for realizing mechano-intelligence in a one-dimensional reconfigurable metastructure. Its high-degree-of-freedom nonlinear dynamics are harnessed as physical computing resource to integrate sensory perception, learning, decision-making, and adaptive action within mechanical domain. By learning the relationships among input conditions, structural responses, and reconfiguration commands, the metastructure can autonomously adapt its configuration to achieve targeted wave functions with minimal electronics. Through analyses and experiments, multiple intelligent functions are demonstrated ranging from self-adaptive wave controls to wave-based logic gates. These results establish physical reservoir computing as a systematic approach for integrating mechano-intelligence and enabling autonomous functional adaptation in engineered structures. Building upon this, the dissertation then advances to a new in-memory phononic learning framework in a two-dimensional multistable metastructure. We introduce non-volatile mechanical memory for information encoding and storage, where spatial information is encoded as structural stable states that program elastic-wave responses, allowing probing waves to act as queries that retrieve informative features through parallel, physically transparent localization modes. Learning is achieved by optimizing input waveforms to selectively combine these features for multitask memory-pattern recognition, with decisions inferred from output energy. We experimentally and numerically demonstrate high-accuracy classification across tasks from geometric shapes to handwritten digits. This study unifies mechanical memory, wave-based perception, learning, and decision-making within a single platform, providing a pathway toward cognitive matter that can interpret, reason, and learn through wave physics. Finally, the dissertation systematically investigates how metastructure properties correlate with physical computing and the resulting mechano-intelligence performance. A broad range of metastructure configurations, design parameters, and operating conditions is evaluated through benchmark temporal-prediction tasks and engineering-relevant frequency-regression and signal-pattern-classification tasks, which reveals how the structural wave dynamics govern physical computing capability and the realization of different intelligent functions. These findings can provide physical insights for designing future mechano-intelligent structures with dynamics tailored to desired functions. Overall, this dissertation provides a basis for creating future intelligent structures that would greatly surpass the state of the art — such as lower power consumption, more direct interactions, and much better survivability in harsh environments or under cyberattacks. Moreover, it suggests a pathway for adding new functions and autonomy to material and structural systems without overburdening onboard computers.

records.title: Reservoir Computing for Pattern Recognition and Time‐Series Prediction Based on Nanofluidic Negative Differential Resistance
records.abstract: Physical reservoir computing (RC) employs the dynamics of a system to obtain a nonlinear representation of the input data that is useful for pattern recognition and complex time‐series forecasting. Here, we propose a new RC method for image classification where the reservoir dynamics makes use of the negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomena in a nanofluidic biomimetic pore caused by salt precipitation. The experimental reservoir consists of charged conical nanopores bathed in salt solutions, and the sequential NDR phenomena are characterized by abrupt drops in the ionic current when the applied voltage exceeds a series of threshold voltages. By exploiting these nonlinear characteristics, we demonstrate theoretically an RC realization that is able to classify a broad range of binary images with high accuracy by using a nanofluidic reservoir. Also, we consider temporal data forecasting using a biologically inspired model of voltage‐gated ion channels with NDR characteristics. To this end, we use two generic inward‐ and outward‐rectifying channels characteristic of biological membranes and test the RC forecasting with the Mackey–Glass chaotic time series.
